concepts.title: Measures of Dispersion
concepts.definition: A single central value cannot say how spread out the observations are, so statistics adds scatter measures: range, quartile deviation, mean deviation and standard deviation. Dispersion about the mean matters most; a distribution where data bunches tightly near the centre shows low dispersion, while widely thrown values show high dispersion.
concepts.key_idea: Central tendency locates the data; dispersion says how far the data strays from that location.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh113.txt lines 30-113 (sections 13.1, 13.2; two batsmen scores example, list of the four dispersion measures)

solution_steps.explain: Means and medians report a typical value, but two series can share a mean while differing wildly in scatter.
Range, quartile deviation, mean deviation and standard deviation each quantify spread differently.
Mean deviation and standard deviation use every observation's distance from the mean, so they are the workhorses for comparison.

concepts.title: Range of a Series
concepts.definition: The range is the quickest scatter read-out: subtract the smallest observation from the largest. It uses only two data points, so it is fast but crude -- two very different data sets can carry the same range.
concepts.key_idea: Largest minus smallest -- one subtraction, but it ignores every value in between.

concepts.title: Mean Deviation About the Mean (Ungrouped Data)
concepts.definition: Mean deviation averages the absolute distances of all observations from the mean: first compute the mean, then average how far each observation sits from it, ignoring signs. Absolute gaps are used because signed deviations from the mean always cancel to zero.
concepts.formula: mad = (abs(x1 - mean) + abs(x2 - mean) + abs(x3 - mean)) / obs_count
concepts.key_idea: Strip the signs, then average -- mean deviation is the typical distance from the centre.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh113.txt lines 131-260 (sections 13.4, 13.4.1 mean deviation for ungrouped data about mean and median)

concepts.title: Mean Deviation for Grouped (Frequency) Data
concepts.definition: For data packaged into a frequency table, each distinct value (or class midpoint) is repeated f times, so the mean is a weighted average and each absolute gap counts f times. The mean deviation is the frequency-weighted total of absolute gaps divided by the total frequency.
concepts.key_idea: Weights change the averaging, not the idea: bigger frequencies pull the mean and carry more deviation weight.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh113.txt lines 261-360 (section 13.4.2 mean deviation for grouped data, discrete and continuous frequency distributions)

solution_steps.explain: Multiply each value (or midpoint) by its frequency, add over all rows, and divide by the total frequency N.
For each row take the absolute gap between the value and the mean and multiply by that row's frequency.
The weighted gap total over N is the mean deviation for the grouped data.

concepts.title: Variance and Standard Deviation
concepts.definition: Variance squares the deviations from the mean before averaging them, which stops positives and negatives cancelling and punishes big misses; the standard deviation is its square root, returning to the original units. A small standard deviation marks data packed near the mean.
concepts.formula: sd = sqrt(((x1 - mean_val) ** 2 + (x2 - mean_val) ** 2 + (x3 - mean_val) ** 2) / obs_count)
concepts.key_idea: Square to kill the cancellation, average, then root back to the data's units -- that root is the standard deviation.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh113.txt lines 361-460 (section 13.5 and 13.5.1 standard deviation as positive square root of variance)

concepts.title: Standard Deviation of a Frequency Distribution
concepts.definition: With frequencies in play, each squared deviation is repeated f times: variance becomes the frequency-weighted mean of squared gaps between values (or class midpoints) and the mean, divided by total frequency N; its square root is the standard deviation of the distribution.
concepts.key_idea: Same squaring recipe, but every term is stamped with its frequency before averaging.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh113.txt lines 461-560 (sections 13.5.2 and 13.5.3, standard deviation of discrete and continuous frequency distributions)

solution_steps.explain: Sum f*x over the table and divide by N, using midpoints for continuous classes.

Divide the weighted total by N for variance, then take the positive square root.

concepts.title: Shortcut Method for Variance via Assumed Mean
concepts.definition: When numbers are awkward, shift the origin: subtract a convenient assumed mean from every observation to get small deviations, square and average those instead, and correct the result. With a common step size h the data can be scaled down further, and the variance comes out as h squared times the mean squared deviation minus the square of the mean deviation of the shifted data.
concepts.key_idea: Shifting the origin simplifies the arithmetic -- compute variance of the small shifted values, then rescale by h squared.

solution_steps.explain: Each observation is reduced by the assumed mean; the mean of those differences is mean_dev.
Squaring each difference first and averaging gives mean_sq_dev.
Subtracting the square of the mean deviation and rescaling by h squared restores the true variance.
